title: Entropy and the Second Law of Thermodynamics
short_intro: Entropy is a state function representing a measure of the unavailability of a system's thermal energy for conversion into mechanical work. Mathematically, it is defined through the macroscopic change dQ/T for a reversible process.

exam_scope.tgt_core: Definition of entropy, Clausius inequality, entropy changes in ideal gas processes (isothermal, isobaric, isochoric, adiabatic), and principle of increase of entropy.
exam_scope.pgt_extension: Statistical interpretation of entropy (Boltzmann relation), entropy of mixing, exact differential property of state functions, and T-S diagram analysis for thermodynamic cycles.

concept_notes.heading: Macroscopic Definition and State Function Nature
bullets: Entropy (S) is an extensive thermodynamic state function, meaning its value depends only on the current state of the system, independent of the path taken.
The infinitesimal change in entropy dS for a reversible process is given by the ratio of heat added reversibly (dQ<sub>rev</sub>) to the absolute temperature (T).
The cyclic integral of dQ/T over any closed reversible cycle is identically zero, proving that entropy is a point function.

concept_notes.heading: Clausius Inequality and the Second Law
bullets: For any arbitrary cycle (reversible or irreversible), the cyclic integral of dQ/T is less than or equal to zero: \oint \frac{dQ}{T} \le 0.
For an irreversible process between two equilibrium states, the entropy change dS > \frac{dQ}{T}.
In an isolated system (dQ = 0), entropy can never decrease; it remains constant for reversible processes (dS = 0) and increases for irreversible processes (dS > 0).

concept_notes.heading: Statistical Interpretation of Entropy
bullets: Boltzmann related macroscopic entropy to microscopic probability through the relation S = k<sub>B</sub> ln(Ω), where k<sub>B</sub> is the Boltzmann constant and Ω is the thermodynamic probability (number of microstates).
Entropy is a measure of the degree of molecular disorder or randomness in a system.
Absolute entropy at T = 0 K is zero for a perfectly crystalline substance (Nernst Heat Theorem / Third Law of Thermodynamics).

concept_notes.heading: T-S Diagrams (Temperature-Entropy)
bullets: A Temperature-Entropy (T-S) diagram plots absolute temperature on the ordinate and entropy on the abscissa.
The area under the T-S curve for a reversible process represents the total heat transferred: Q = \int T dS.
Isothermal processes appear as horizontal lines on a T-S diagram, whereas isentropic (reversible adiabatic) processes appear as vertical lines.

derivations.title: Entropy Change of an Ideal Gas
derivations.conditions: One mole of an ideal gas undergoing a state change from (T<sub>1</sub>, V<sub>1</sub>) to (T<sub>2</sub>, V<sub>2</sub>)
steps: Start from the first law of thermodynamics for a closed system: dQ = dU + dW
Substitute dU = C<sub>V</sub> dT and dW = P dV = \frac{RT}{V} dV into the expression: dQ = C_V dT + \frac{RT}{V} dV
Divide by absolute temperature T to obtain the entropy change: dS = \frac{dQ}{T} = C_V \frac{dT}{T} + R \frac{dV}{V}
Integrate between initial state (T<sub>1</sub>, V<sub>1</sub>) and final state (T<sub>2</sub>, V<sub>2</sub>): \Delta S = \int_{T_1}^{T_2} C_V \frac{dT}{T} + \int_{V_1}^{V_2} R \frac{dV}{V}

derivations.title: Entropy Change during Phase Transition
derivations.conditions: Reversible phase change at constant temperature T and pressure P (e.g., melting or vaporization)
steps: During a phase change, the temperature remains constant at the transition temperature T<sub>t</sub>.
The heat supplied reversibly is equal to the latent heat of transition (L): Q = L.
Substitute into the definition of entropy change: \Delta S = \int \frac{dQ_{rev}}{T} = \frac{1}{T_t} \int dQ
Evaluate the integral for mass m with latent heat L.

graphs_and_experiments.title: Carnot Cycle on T-S Diagram
graphs_and_experiments.what_to_draw: A rectangle on the T-S plane bounded by two isotherms (horizontal lines) and two isentropes (vertical lines).
graphs_and_experiments.interpretation: The enclosed rectangular area represents the net work done (or net heat absorbed) in one complete Carnot cycle.
graphs_and_experiments.exam_use: Frequently tested in PGT/TGT for visualizing cycle efficiency and work output directly from thermal coordinates.

graphs_and_experiments.title: Throttling Process (Joule-Thomson Expansion)
graphs_and_experiments.what_to_draw: Enthalpy is constant (h<sub>1</sub> = h<sub>2</sub>), but entropy increases as pressure drops across a porous plug.
graphs_and_experiments.interpretation: Throttling is a highly irreversible process; hence \Delta S > 0 even though no heat is exchanged with the surroundings (adiabatic).
graphs_and_experiments.exam_use: Tested conceptually to verify that adiabatic does not imply isentropic if the process is irreversible.

graphs_and_experiments.title: Entropy vs Temperature for a Solid
graphs_and_experiments.what_to_draw: An increasing curve starting from S = 0 at T = 0 K, rising steeply and then leveling off according to Debye's T<sup>3</sup> law at very low temperatures.
graphs_and_experiments.interpretation: Validates the Third Law of Thermodynamics and illustrates how vibrational degrees of freedom populate with thermal energy.
graphs_and_experiments.exam_use: Used in PGT questions linking specific heat capacity measurements at low temperatures to absolute entropy.

solved_numericals.question: Calculate the change in entropy when 2 kg of water at 100 °C is converted into steam at the same temperature. Given the latent heat of vaporization of water is 2.26 × 10<sup>6</sup> J kg<sup>-1</sup>.
solution_steps: Identify given values: Mass m = 2 kg, Temperature T = 100 °C = 373.15 K, Latent heat L = 2.26 × 10<sup>6</sup> J kg<sup>-1</sup>.
Apply the formula for entropy change during phase transition: \Delta S = \frac{m L}{T}
Calculate the final numerical value: \Delta S \approx 12112.8 \text{ J K}^{-1}

solved_numericals.question: One mole of an ideal monatomic gas (C<sub>V</sub> = 3/2 R) is heated from 300 K to 600 K while its volume is doubled. Calculate the total entropy change of the gas. (Take R = 8.314 J mol<sup>-1</sup> K<sup>-1</sup>, ln 2 = 0.693)
solution_steps: Identify given values: n = 1, T<sub>1</sub> = 300 K, T<sub>2</sub> = 600 K, V<sub>2</sub> / V<sub>1</sub> = 2, C<sub>V</sub> = 1.5 R.
Use the entropy change formula for an ideal gas: \Delta S = C_V \ln\left(\frac{T_2}{T_1}\right) + R \ln\left(\frac{V_2}{V_1}\right)
Substitute C<sub>V</sub> = 1.5 R: \Delta S = 1.5 R \ln(2) + R \ln(2) = 2.5 R \ln(2)
Calculate the result: \Delta S \approx 14.41 \text{ J K}^{-1}

solved_numericals.question: A block of copper of mass 1 kg and specific heat capacity 400 J kg<sup>-1</sup> K<sup>-1</sup> is heated from 27 °C to 127 °C. Find the entropy change of the copper block.
solution_steps: Convert temperatures to Kelvin: T<sub>1</sub> = 27 + 273 = 300 K, T<sub>2</sub> = 127 + 273 = 400 K.
Use the entropy change formula for a solid/liquid: \Delta S = \int \frac{m c dT}{T} = m c \ln\left(\frac{T_2}{T_1}\right)
Calculate final value: \Delta S = 400 \times 0.2877 \approx 115.08 \text{ J K}^{-1}

assumptions_and_limitations: Macroscopic entropy calculations via dQ/T assume the process can be approximated or executed as a reversible path between equilibrium end-states.
The ideal gas formulas assume constant specific heats C<sub>V</sub> and C<sub>P</sub> over the temperature range considered.

common_misconceptions.wrong: Adiabatic processes are always isentropic (constant entropy).
common_misconceptions.correct: Only reversible adiabatic processes are isentropic. Irreversible adiabatic processes (like free expansion or throttling) involve an increase in entropy.
common_misconceptions.why: Irreversibility generates internal entropy even when no external heat is exchanged.

common_misconceptions.wrong: Entropy of a system can never decrease under any circumstance.
common_misconceptions.correct: The entropy of a specific system can decrease (e.g., when water freezes into ice), but the entropy of the universe (system + surroundings) must always increase or remain constant.
common_misconceptions.why: Heat released to the surroundings during freezing increases the surroundings' entropy by a greater or equal amount.

quick_revision: Entropy is an extensive state function defined by dS = dQ<sub>rev</sub> / T with units J K<sup>-1</sup>.
For any natural (irreversible) process in an isolated system, dS > 0.
Boltzmann statistical relation links entropy to microstates: S = k<sub>B</sub> ln(Ω).
On a T-S diagram, area under the curve represents reversible heat transfer.
